question: The European shipbuilding industry is an extremely important economic sector1 and of huge significance from the point of view of security. Some 80% of Europe’s foreign trade is carried by sea. However, Europe has lost control over entire production sectors that are key to the functioning of the European shipbuilding industry, mainly to China, as a result of many years of policy mistakes by the EU institutions.

The situation of steel producers (the main shipbuilding sub-suppliers) is also deteriorating. European steel mills are collapsing under the burden of obligations resulting from the European Green Deal, and production is being relocated to countries that are not subject to CO2 emissions standards.

The production capacity of Chinese shipyards is currently 10 times higher than the combined production capacity of EU and US shipyards. China supports its shipbuilding industry with subsidies, puts up protectionist barriers and ensures access to finance on favourable terms, treating shipbuilding as a strategic industry. These measures are not available to European producers.
Furthermore, China is pragmatically addressing climate issues, avoiding imposing additional financial burdens on its economy, unlike the EU and the Green Deal package. 1.

Does the Commission plan to review the burden on the European shipbuilding sector resulting from the Green Deal, which could lead to the complete collapse of this sector of the European economy and result in total dependence on China in this area?
Does the Commission recognise the negative effects of the Green Deal for EU security, including the situation of naval shipyards?
How does the Commission plan to support the European shipbuilding industry in the context of unfair competition from China?

In the EU there are around 300 shipyards. The sector employs some 1.1 million people and generates commercial and military sales worth around EUR 128 billion. It accounts for 24% of the value of global shipbuilding production, thanks to its very strong position in the manufacture of ship equipment and production for naval requirements.
answer: The EU shipbuilding sector’s competitiveness challenges are not caused by the Green Deal, which can offer opportunities by stimulating fleet modernisation investments (2) as also highlighted in the mobility transition pathway (3). In parallel, the Commission will continue to monitor and support the sector’s competitive position.

The Commission is not informed of evidence-based negative effects of the Green Deal on EU security and supports a strong European defence technological and industrial base (4), including in the naval domain, inter alia through the European Defence Fund (5) and the new European Defence Industrial Strategy (6).

The Commission is engaged in a constant dialogue with industry and other stakeholders to identify potential measures that can support the European shipbuilding industry in its transformation. It has already taken various actions that will support the sector (7).

For example, the revenue from auctioning 20 million EU Emissions Trading System allowances will be available up to 2030 through the Innovation Fund to support maritime decarbonisation projects, including innovation in the shipbuilding sector with a clear EU-added value.
The Commission remains committed to leveraging all tools at its disposal to preserve the sector’s global competitiveness and technological leadership.

In the EU there are around 300 shipyards. The sector employs some 1.1 million people and generates commercial and military sales worth around EUR 128 billion. It accounts for 24% of the value of global shipbuilding production, thanks to its very strong position in the manufacture of ship equipment and production for naval requirements.
